title: Ear
shortDescription: The outer, middle, and inner ear structures, and how they enable both hearing and balance.
genZNote: Helps you hear and balance — one organ, two completely different jobs.

illustration.alt: Labelled cross-section illustration of the ear
illustration.caption: Ear — Cellfie Human Anatomy

structures.name: Pinna
structures.description: The visible outer part of the ear.
structures.function: Collects and funnels sound waves into the ear canal.

structures.name: Ear canal
structures.description: Tube leading from the pinna to the eardrum.
structures.function: Channels sound waves toward the eardrum.

structures.name: Eardrum (tympanic membrane)
structures.description: Thin membrane at the end of the ear canal.
structures.function: Vibrates in response to sound waves.

structures.name: Malleus
structures.description: First of the three ossicles (middle ear bones).
structures.function: Transmits vibration from the eardrum to the incus.

structures.name: Incus
structures.function: Passes vibration from the malleus to the stapes.

structures.name: Stapes
structures.description: Smallest bone in the body; last of the three ossicles.

structures.name: Cochlea
structures.description: Spiral, fluid-filled structure in the inner ear.
structures.function: Converts vibrations into neural signals for hearing.

structures.name: Semicircular canals
structures.description: Three fluid-filled loops in the inner ear.
structures.function: Detect head rotation and movement, maintaining balance.

structures.name: Eustachian tube
structures.description: Tube connecting the middle ear to the throat.
structures.function: Equalizes air pressure between the middle ear and the outside environment.

comparisons.distinction: The cochlea converts vibrations into hearing signals; the semicircular canals detect rotation/movement for balance.
The three ossicles mechanically transmit vibration through the middle ear; the cochlea then converts that vibration into a neural signal in the inner ear.

questions.prompt: In the labelled ear illustration, which structure detects head rotation for balance, not hearing?
questions.explanation: The semicircular canals detect rotation and movement of the head, contributing to balance, while the cochlea handles hearing.
optionNotes: Vibrates with sound, part of the hearing pathway.
Equalizes pressure, unrelated to balance detection.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order of the three ossicles, from the eardrum inward?
questions.explanation: Vibration travels malleus → incus → stapes, from the eardrum toward the cochlea.

sections.heading: Structures of the Ear
bullets: Pinna — the visible outer ear; collects sound.
Ear canal — channels sound waves toward the eardrum.
Eardrum (tympanic membrane) — vibrates in response to sound waves.
Malleus, incus, stapes — three tiny middle-ear bones (ossicles) that amplify and relay vibrations.
Cochlea — the fluid-filled, spiral inner-ear structure that converts vibrations into nerve signals for hearing.
Semicircular canals — inner-ear structures that detect head rotation and movement, key to balance.
Eustachian tube — connects the middle ear to the throat, equalizing air pressure.

rows: Sound vibrations converted to nerve signals

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: The ear enables hearing via the cochlea and balance via the semicircular canals, with sound first amplified by the outer and middle ear structures.
keyFacts: Sound path: pinna → ear canal → eardrum → ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) → cochlea.
The cochlea converts sound vibrations into nerve signals; it is not involved in balance.
Semicircular canals, not the cochlea, are responsible for balance.
The Eustachian tube equalizes pressure between the middle ear and the throat.
commonConfusion: Cochlea (hearing) and semicircular canals (balance) are both inner-ear structures but serve entirely different senses.

highYieldFacts: The three ossicles, in order, are malleus, incus, then stapes.
Balance is a function of the semicircular canals, not the cochlea.
commonTraps: Don't assign balance to the cochlea — it is purely for hearing.
mustRemember: Sound pathway: pinna → ear canal → eardrum → malleus → incus → stapes → cochlea → brain.
